cards.starter: A tiny campsite rescue beacon is dark. A wire almost reaches the battery. Can almost-connected electricity light the beacon?

cards.question: Will the red LED glow if its return wire never reaches battery negative?
choices: Yes, the gap is small enough
Not sure; I want to test it
cards.why_prompt: Why do you think so? A sketch, spoken answer or “not sure yet” is welcome.

cards.starter: After an adult checks the completed loop, connect the 3 V holder and observe the LED. Disconnect the holder. Open only the return connection, keep the loose end away from other conductors, then reconnect power and observe. Disconnect before restoring the wire. Keep the LED, resistor and batteries the same.

cards.observation_prompt: Record closed / open / restored as three separate trials, with what you actually saw, even if the result was unexpected.

cards.starter: Your light needs a complete conducting route from one battery terminal, through the resistor and LED, to the other terminal. We call this route a **circuit**. In our low-voltage build, an air gap stops the current, even when the wire is very close. The battery supplies energy; the LED changes some of that energy into light. The resistor limits the current so the LED can work safely. Closing the route is necessary, but it is not the only requirement: the LED must face the correct way and the batteries must still have enough energy. Which observation supported or changed your prediction?
cards.explorer: The same current passes through each part of this series loop. A rough estimate with a 3 V source, a 2 V red LED drop and 220 Ω is (3−2)/220 ≈ 4.5 mA; actual parts vary. The resistor limits current, rather than making the battery send exactly one fixed current. The LED is polarized. An open loop prevents sustained current in this particular circuit.
cards.unlock_note: Offer after an observation attempt; allow mentor override and review later.

cards.starter: A switch gives you a way to choose whether a circuit has a complete path. In this design, closing the flap brings two foil contacts together. Current can then pass through the switch, resistor and LED, so the light glows. Opening the flap separates the contacts and breaks the path. The light goes out. The foil is part of the path, so it must stay away from any connection that could bypass the resistor or short the battery. Compare your open and closed observations. Did the flap control the light reliably, or did a loose contact sometimes interrupt it?
cards.explorer: An ideal closed switch has low resistance. Real foil contacts can add resistance or make an intermittent connection. This is a closing-trigger mechanism. An opening-trigger alarm would require a different reviewed switch arrangement.

cards.starter: A material can help complete a circuit if it lets enough current pass through our tester. We call a material that does this a conductor. A dry metal paperclip often makes the light glow, while dry plastic usually does not. Some objects have coatings that stop good contact, even when the material underneath conducts. A dark LED therefore means only that this test did not show enough current for visible light. It does not prove an object has absolutely no conductivity. Compare your predictions with the observations for each object. Which result would you repeat before making a claim?
cards.explorer: This is a qualitative, low-voltage conductivity indicator. Contact resistance, surface coatings, source condition and LED visibility affect results. No-light is a detection limit, not a numerical resistance measurement.

cards.starter: An LED has two different terminals. Its orientation matters because current passes through it readily in one direction. In our 3 V circuit, the red LED glows when its anode faces battery positive through the resistor and its cathode returns to negative. Reversing it usually stops visible light. The resistor stays in the loop for both tests. Long and short legs can help identify a new LED, but trimmed legs lose that clue. An adult must check the actual part. Your forward, reversed and restored trials test orientation while keeping the other parts the same. Which observation best supports your explanation?
cards.explorer: LEDs are polarized semiconductor diodes. Reverse-voltage tolerance varies by part. This activity is limited to the isolated reviewed 3 V red-LED kit. Never generalize the reversal test to higher voltage or unspecified parts.

cards.starter: Parallel branches provide separate paths between the same battery terminals. Each path in this project contains its own resistor and red LED. Opening one branch stops current in that branch while the other path can stay complete. That is why one window can stay lit when the other goes dark. The branches share a battery, so a weak source can still affect both. Each LED needs its own current-limiting resistor. Do not connect bare LEDs across the battery or put both parallel LEDs behind one shared resistor. Your one-branch-at-a-time test shows which paths depend on each connection.
cards.explorer: Each branch spans the source voltage and independently limits its LED current. This 3 V kit does not reliably light two red LEDs in series, so it intentionally avoids a physical series comparison.

cards.starter: Your Arduino follows a sequence of instructions. The setup function runs once when the board starts. The loop function repeats. Our sketch turns the built-in LED on, waits, turns it off and waits again. Shorter waits make each whole cycle take less time, so more cycles fit into ten seconds. Changing code lets you test a prediction without changing any wires. The light labeled L is different from power and communication lights that may also appear on the board. Compare the same built-in light in both trials. What would happen if you shortened only the on-time?

cards.starter: Code can organize several outputs into a repeatable sequence. Each traffic-light color has its own output pin and its own resistor. If only green lasts longer, the total cycle also lasts longer. The physical circuit stays the same while you change one timing value. A tabletop model helps you investigate sequences, but real traffic control needs many additional safety rules. Which observation shows that your code change affected timing rather than wiring?

cards.question: With INPUT_PULLUP and a button to GND, what will D2 read when you press?
choices: Not sure; I want to test it
cards.why_prompt: Why do you think so? A sketch, spoken answer or “not sure yet” is welcome.

cards.starter: Run the provided sketch and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. Compare one released reading with one pressed reading without changing wires. Record the words and the LED state before revealing the explanation. Keep the same button, sketch and pins.

cards.observation_prompt: Record cycle number, released input/LED, pressed input/LED and one unexpected result.

cards.starter: A computer input needs a clear electrical state. Without a helpful connection it might give an uncertain reading. The setting **INPUT_PULLUP** uses a resistor inside the Arduino to hold D2 HIGH when the button is released. Pressing our normally-open button joins D2 to GND, so it reads LOW. The sketch checks for LOW and turns the separate LED output HIGH. The input and output do different jobs: LOW can mean “pressed” while HIGH means “light on.” This is a rule we chose in code. Compare your pressed and released readings: did they support your prediction, or did you discover a different rule?
cards.explorer: The internal pull-up limits current from 5 V when the button grounds D2. A four-leg tactile switch often has two permanently connected pins per electrical contact; identify the actual switched pair while unpowered. This sketch responds to level, not one event per press. Mechanical bounce matters for later toggle/reaction games and is not solved simply by INPUT_PULLUP.
cards.unlock_note: Offer after an observation attempt; allow mentor override and review later.

cards.starter: The Arduino can switch an output on and off faster than you usually notice. Pulse-width modulation, or PWM, changes how much of each repeating interval the output stays on. More on-time usually makes this LED look brighter. The values in analogWrite choose that on-time pattern on a supported pin such as D9 on our Uno R3. They do not turn D9 into a smoothly adjustable analog voltage source. Your eyes also do not judge brightness in a perfectly even scale. Compare the low, middle and high settings by observation. What stays the same in your circuit while the light appears to change?
cards.explorer: Uno R3 analogWrite uses a 0–255 duty command on PWM pins. PWM is a switching waveform. Apparent brightness depends on LED current, optics and vision, so equal command changes need not look equally bright.

cards.starter: A repeating vibration can make sound. Frequency tells us how often the vibration repeats each second. With our quiet passive piezo, a higher frequency usually sounds like a higher pitch. Duration is different: it tells us how long the signal continues. A short-long pattern can carry a message even when the pitch stays the same. Some learners prefer a silent light pattern, which can teach timing without sound. Both choices let you make a signal and check whether another person can recognize it. Which part of your message depends on duration, and which part depends on pitch?

cards.starter: A reaction game needs clear states. First it waits for a released button. Then it waits for an unpredictable cue. A press before the cue counts as a false start. After the light appears, the program measures elapsed time until the next accepted press. The millis clock lets the sketch keep checking the input while time passes. An unpredictable delay makes anticipation harder, but it does not make every trial perfectly fair. Button mechanics, display timing and practice affect results. Your best evidence is a repeated set of trials with the same rules. What should the machine do if someone holds the button down before the game begins?
cards.explorer: The sketch uses debounced edges and unsigned elapsed-time subtraction. A false start requires release before another trial. Pseudorandom waits reduce predictability but are not secure randomness. Timing includes debounce latency and software sampling.

cards.question: Which push point will feel easier with the same load: 6 cm or 14 cm from the pivot?
choices: Not sure; I want to test it
cards.why_prompt: Why do you think so? A sketch, spoken answer or “not sure yet” is welcome.

cards.starter: With the same paper load 6 cm to the left of the pivot, press downward first 6 cm, then 14 cm to the right. Lift the load to the same small marked height each time. Repeat in the opposite order. Record “easier / similar / harder”; light loads or friction may make the difference hard to feel. Do not add heavy weights.
cards.variable: Effort distance from pivot: 6 cm versus 14 cm
cards.keep_constant: Same load, load-arm distance, pivot, direction and target lift height.
cards.observation_prompt: Record effort point, same target reached?, feeling, and how far the hand moved. A drawing or spoken explanation is valid.

cards.starter: A **lever** is a stiff piece that turns around a pivot. Your push turns one side down and lifts the other side. Pushing farther from the pivot can make the same paper load feel easier to lift. There is a tradeoff: your hand travels farther to lift the load the same height. The lever does not create energy. It changes how force and movement distance fit together. Real cardboard bends and pivots rub, so the result may not match a perfect lever. If your two trials felt similar, that is useful evidence too. Can you point to the part you changed and the parts you kept the same?
cards.explorer: For a slow, approximately balanced lever, effort force × perpendicular effort arm ≈ load force × perpendicular load arm, plus friction effects. With a 6 cm load arm and a 14 cm effort arm, ideal effort is about 6/14 of the load force; with both arms 6 cm, it is about equal. The longer effort side moves through a greater arc length for the same angular turn. Feeling force is qualitative, not a precise measurement.
cards.unlock_note: Offer after an observation attempt; allow mentor override and review later.

cards.starter: A linkage joins stiff pieces with pivots so their movements depend on each other. When you turn one piece, the connections guide where another point can travel. Moving a pivot changes the geometry, so the path can change even when your hand makes the same movement. Cardboard flex and loose fasteners also affect the line. cards.starter: A servo uses a control signal to aim its shaft toward a requested position. Our Arduino sends that signal while a separate adult-prepared supply provides the servo power. We use a light paper arm, a limited tested angle range and clear space around it. Command numbers are targets, not proof of exact physical angles. cards.starter: After the checked build and upload, open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. Record three room-light values, shade the LDR with dry card without moving wires, and record three values after settling. Remove shade and repeat. cards.starter: A photoresistor changes its resistance when light reaches it. It usually has less resistance in brighter light. Our **voltage divider** joins the photoresistor above a fixed resistor, with A0 measuring the meeting point. With this arrangement, brighter light usually makes the meeting point voltage higher, so A0 reports a larger number. Shading usually makes the number smaller. These readings are clues about this circuit, not a precise light meter. Different parts and rooms give different ranges. Compare your groups of readings rather than searching for one magic number. Did removing the shade bring the numbers back toward their first group? That repeat test helps you decide whether light caused the change.
cards.explorer: For this orientation, Vjunction = 5 V × 10 kΩ/(RLDR + 10 kΩ). As RLDR falls in light, the junction voltage rises. The Uno R3 analogRead result is a nominal 10-bit number, 0–1023, relative to its reference; it is not calibrated lux. Reversing the divider reverses the trend, which is why diagrams must specify component positions. Compare ranges and repeat conditions before selecting later thresholds.

cards.starter: An NTC thermistor changes resistance as its temperature changes. NTC means its resistance usually goes down as it warms. cards.starter: A dark light is an observation, not a diagnosis. An open wire and a reversed LED can both make this circuit dark. **Fault isolation** means choosing a small test that separates possible causes. Start with the known-good diagram, inspect one feature, and make one safe change with the battery disconnected. Then compare the result with your prediction. lessons.mentor_note: No publishing requirement. Adult checks the demonstration and any media. Keep feedback respectful, voluntary and local.

support_modes.Starter: Read one action at a time. A mentor can read aloud, prepare software and handle safety checks. Choose your own prediction and describe your observations.
support_modes.Explorer: Local communication is the completion route. Guest publishing and media uploads remain disabled. A future public version requires guardian approval and human moderation, including a separate privacy review of media and metadata.
support_modes.Inventor: Communicate the main idea without powering the prototype, using a diagram and test log. Keep the same safety limits and state your success target first.

mentor_questions.question: What changes in this experiment?
mentor_questions.answer: One improvement suggested during local feedback

mentor_questions.question: What should stay the same?
mentor_questions.answer: Same prototype, stated target and test conditions.

mentor_questions.question: What evidence should I look for?
mentor_questions.answer: A listener can explain your problem, one piece of evidence and the reason for a design change.

mentor_questions.question: What if it still does not work?
mentor_questions.answer: Stop safely, record the actual result and justify one next safe test. Ask the mentor for the appropriate hint.

mentor_questions.question: How can I extend it?
mentor_questions.answer: Communicate the main idea without powering the prototype, using a diagram and test log.

lessons.cleanup: Disconnect all electrical sources first, or stop mechanical movement. Let the adult inspect parts. Count the reusable components, cover fastener points and store small parts away from younger children.
lessons.sequence_note: Build the adult-checked setup after predicting, then experiment and reveal. The content model retains nine card kinds, with Build moved earlier to avoid testing nonexistent hardware.
